message.content:
Lions (Panthera leo) belong to the family **Felidae** in the order **Carnivora**, while zebras (Equus quagga) belong to the family **Equidae** in the order **Perissodactyla**.  
Their most recent common ancestor is therefore the last common ancestor of the two major clades that give rise to modern carnivorans and perissodactyls – a small, probably insect‑eating mammal that lived when those two lineages split off from each other.  

That split occurred in the late Cretaceous/early Paleogene, roughly **70–90 million years ago**. In other words, the last common ancestor of lions and zebras was a very early placental mammal that predated the diversification of the modern orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla.
message.reasoning:
The user asks: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" They want an answer. We can provide a general evolutionary biology answer: The common ancestor of lions (Panthera leo) and zebras (Equus quagga) would be a common ancestor within the order Carnivora? Wait, lions are mammals in the family Felidae, subfamily Pantherinae. Zebras are equids, family Equidae. Both belong to class Mammalia, but their last common ancestor would be at the level of the order level? Actually, lions are in order Carnivora, while zebras are in order Perissodactyla. So the last common ancestor would be at the level of the clade Eutheria (placental mammals). But maybe they want the last common ancestor of the two species: the last common ancestor of lions and zebras would be a mammal from the group of early placentals, perhaps around 70 million years ago. But we could mention that the last common ancestor of all modern mammals is the common ancestor of the clades that gave rise to carnivores and perissodactyls. That might be the last common ancestor of the clades Carnivora and Perissodactyla, which diverged around 100 million years ago. But the question likely expects something like "the last common ancestor of lions and zebras was a small, early mammal that lived about 70 million years ago." Or "the last common ancestor of lions and zebras was a member of the clade Afrotheria"? No, that's wrong.

We should answer with a concise explanation: The last common ancestor of lions and zebras is a mammalian ancestor that existed before the divergence of the orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla, roughly 80–90 million years ago. Provide context: Lions are part of the family Felidae, order Carnivora; zebras are part of the family Equidae, order Perissodactyla. Their last common ancestor would have been a small, probably insectivorous mammal that lived during the late Cretaceous or early Paleogene. Provide approximate time frame: ~70–80 million years ago. Also mention that the last common ancestor of all placental mammals is older (~160–200 million years ago). But the last common ancestor of the two specific lineages is more recent.

Thus answer accordingly.
